note.question: How does process automation shape behavioral externalities?
note.overview: Two workers make repeated work-versus-delay choices on sequential tasks whose completion determines both players' project payoff. The paper derives the subgame-perfect equilibrium by backward induction, adds strategic uncertainty about a coworker's rationality, and tests the resulting predictions against human-human and human-robot play.

components.label: Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the finite-horizon sequential-task game
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Subgame-perfect equilibrium of the finite-horizon sequential-task game. The authors explicitly solve backward from the downstream task and characterize W2's and then W1's optimal strategy in Propositions 1-2. Every history is covered by the remaining-work and time state, so the prescribed policies are sequentially optimal in each continuation game.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Over periods t=1,...,T, task 1 is active until Worker 1 supplies tau_1 work periods; task 2 then becomes active until Worker 2 supplies tau_2 work periods. At the start of each active period the human observes the current outside option and chooses work or delay. If task 2 finishes by T, both workers receive the project value plus an early-completion bonus; otherwise the project payoff is zero. Only one task is active at a time, so Worker 1's speed determines when Worker 2 can begin.

components.explanation: The paper solves the normative game by dynamic programming and backward induction, derives a belief-based behavioral policy for the upstream worker, and implements the environment in two incentivized experiments.
